# On Desire Paths

There's a particular kind of trail you've seen a thousand times without having a name for it. A park has a paved walkway that curves elegantly around a lawn, and cutting straight across the grass is a bare strip of dirt, worn smooth by feet. Planners call these *desire paths*, a phrase that's almost embarrassingly poetic for the field of landscape architecture.

I find them quietly moving, and I've been trying to work out why.

Part of it is that a desire path is a record no one intended to make. Nobody decides to create one. Each person just wants to get to the bus stop a few seconds faster, or the pavement was icy, or they were late, or the curve felt fussy and pointless that morning. Individually, these are tiny acts of impatience. Collectively, they carve a line into the earth that says, with total clarity: *this is where people actually want to go.* It's a vote nobody knew they were casting.

There's a story, possibly apocryphal, as the best design stories tend to be, about a university that built its campus without any sidewalks. The administrators waited a year, watched where the grass died, and then paved those lines. Whether it happened exactly that way, several places have tried versions of it. The idea has an appealing humility: *we don't know how you'll live here, so we'll let you show us.*

The opposite response is also common. Planners see the dirt track and put up a little fence, or a sign, or a hedge. Sometimes this is justified. Maybe the shortcut crosses fragile ground, or leads people into traffic. But often the fence is a small monument to the belief that the plan was right and the people are wrong. And people, in my experience of reading about these things, mostly just step over the fence. The path gets a little wider on either side of it.

---

I think desire paths are interesting because they sit right on a tension that shows up everywhere: the gap between how a system is designed and how it's used.

Software has desire paths. People use spreadsheets as databases, email as a to-do list, and the "notes to self" chat as a filing cabinet. Language has them too. Grammarians draw careful curves, and speakers cut across the lawn. "Literally" now sometimes means "figuratively," to the despair of many. Singular "they" has been worn smooth by centuries of feet. Dictionaries, eventually, pave it.

Cities are full of them in less literal forms: the stairwell everyone uses as a meeting spot, the loading dock that became a smoking area, the library that became a daytime shelter because it was the only warm public place with a bathroom. That last one is a desire path worth paying attention to. It tells you something about a need the city didn't plan for.

The lesson isn't that designers should never impose structure. The paved curve exists for reasons: drainage, accessibility, a view someone thought was worth slowing down for. Sometimes the long way really is better, and people just haven't noticed. A good path can teach you to see something. But the dirt line is data, and it's unusually honest data, because nobody is performing for it. People lie in surveys. They don't lie with their feet.

---

What I like most, I think, is the way desire paths blur the line between individual and collective. No single person made that trail. If you asked any one of the walkers, they'd say they were just cutting across. But the path exists, and it's shaped like a consensus. It's democratic in a strange, wordless way, with no deliberation, no persuasion, no speeches. Just thousands of small, private decisions that happen to point the same direction.

There's something reassuring in that. People are often described as chaotic, selfish, impossible to coordinate. And yet here's evidence that, left alone, strangers will converge on the same sensible line without ever speaking to each other. The path is a kind of agreement that emerged instead of being negotiated.

Of course, it's also a little melancholy. Every desire path is a small indictment of a plan that didn't quite understand its people. Every one says: *you drew the curve beautifully, and we didn't want it.*

---

If I could suggest one habit, it would be this: next time you see a strip of worn grass cutting a corner, stop and look at where it goes. Ask what the planners assumed and what the walkers knew. It's one of the few places in the world where you can literally see the difference between what people were told to want and what they actually wanted, written in dirt, in a straight line, for anyone to read.

With total freedom here, I want to pick something genuinely interesting to write about with my own voice—maybe octopus arms tasting, the word "sonder," coastline paradoxes, or moss, something concrete and rich rather than generic.

Actually, I'm drawn to "desire paths"—those unofficial trails people carve when the designed path doesn't match how they actually move. It connects design, human behavior, and humility in a way I can weave a genuine essay around, moderate length with real texture.
